clue.text: Swimmer twisted one foot, caught in a rush of water

indicators.note: something caught in a thing is held inside it, so the turned pair goes inside the rush of water

parts.note: a flash is a sudden rush of water, as in a flash flood

indicators.note: twisted round, the short pair of one and foot is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
FT is the standard abbreviation for foot as a measure

explanation.surface: A swimmer turns an ankle after being swept up in a sudden flood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' is any fish here, not a person; 'twisted' gives TFI, which 'caught in' places after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaice or sole is a fish that swims and is flattened in shape, so a swimmer fits as a definition by example.

clue.text: Woman knocked back beer — about one litre

indicators.note: knocked back, like a drink downed, here sends the whole assembly in reverse
the beer goes about the one, wrapping it

parts.note: ale is a beer
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A woman downs a beer, about a litre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts I inside ALE to make ALIE; with L added, 'knocked back' turns ALIEL around.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a female given name, so any woman bearing it fits the definition by example.

clue.text: Endless exciting pulp penned by late author

indicators.note: penned by means held inside, as in a pen

parts.note: tardy means late

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: hot can mean exciting, as in a hot story
to mash something is to pulp it

explanation.surface: A late novelist's work, once thrilling, is now endless pulp fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' is wordplay, not part of the definition, though the novelist is indeed dead; 'Endless' makes HO, and both pieces are 'penned by' the late word after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian novelist and poet wrote Tess of the d'Urbervilles, so he is an author.

clue.text: Break during part of Edinburgh festival

parts.note: in means during, as in in the morning
the Fringe is the open-access arts festival held alongside the Edinburgh International Festival

explanation.surface: A break taken during the Edinburgh festival.
explanation.walkthrough: The Edinburgh Fringe is a huge Scottish arts festival held every August.
explanation.definitionFit: To violate a rule or law is to break it, the verb sense here.

clue.text: Keeps mum and daughter in unusually long stone house

indicators.note: the daughter goes in the jumbled letters
unusually means the letters are arranged in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Mother and daughter live in an unusually long stone house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mum' looks like mother, but 'keeps mum' means stays silent. 'unusually' scrambles LONG STONE HOUSE, and D goes 'in'. 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep mum is to stay silent and say nothing, the same idiom in other words.

clue.text: After half time most of match is lacking in quality

indicators.note: after places the half of time first, followed by the trimmed match word
only half of the word time is wanted, here its second pair of letters
most of a word means all but its final letter

parts.note: to match is to agree or correspond

explanation.surface: A football report: after the half-time break, most of the match was poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half time' looks like the football interval but gives the back half of the word; 'most of' makes AGRE, and 'After' sets the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scanty or poor in amount or substance is lacking in quality, the usual sense of this adjective.

clue.text: Unsuccessful fellow definitely lacks appeal

parts.note: a fellow is a man

indicators.note: lacks means the word goes without the named letters

parts.note: quite can mean definitely, as in quite so
it is sex appeal, as in she's got it

explanation.surface: A failed man who definitely has no charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacks' drops IT from QUITE to give QUE. 'appeal' is the old slang 'it', meaning sex appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed after a noun, this French borrowing means one who failed to become what they hoped, as in a poet unrealised.

clue.text: Everyone bound by international law

indicators.note: bound by means held within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Every nation is bound by international law.
explanation.definitionFit: Everybody or the whole lot of people, the pronoun sense of the word.

clue.text: Flag Edward raised in surrender

indicators.note: the raised name goes in the word for surrender

parts.note: to resign is to give up or surrender

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so the name runs backwards

parts.note: Ned is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: A flag is raised as Edward surrenders.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'raised' reads the name upwards, giving DEN; 'in' places it after the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Ensign is the flag flown by British merchant ships.

clue.text: Dandy wearing suit back to front? Advice needed

indicators.note: back to front tells us to read the whole assembled piece in the opposite direction
the dandy is wearing the suit, so the suit word wraps round the dandy word

parts.note: to suit is to fit, be right for
a fop is a dandy, a man vain about his clothes

explanation.surface: A dandy has put his suit on backwards and needs some advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' gives FFOPIT and 'back to front' turns it round; the question mark flags the jokey reading. 'needed' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip-off is a piece of advance information or warning given privately, a form of advice.

clue.text: Letter from twin boys touring north, heading for Yorkshire

indicators.note: one boy is touring round the north, so the north letter goes inside the first boy

parts.note: a lad is a boy; twin boys gives two of them
N is the compass abbreviation for north
the second of the twin lads

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A letter from twin brothers on a trip north, bound for Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' is not a written message but one who lets rooms. 'touring' puts N inside the first LAD to make LAND.
explanation.definitionFit: One who lets out property is literally a letter, and a woman who lets rooms is the classic example.

clue.text: Miss a swimming competition

parts.note: a miss is a young woman or girl, informally a gal

explanation.surface: A young woman enters a swimming race.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a sporting event, especially in Britain a swimming meet between clubs or schools.

clue.text: Not concerned by current NUS action getting out of hand

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current in physics

indicators.note: things getting out of hand become disordered, so the letters here are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the National Union of Students, taken as written

explanation.surface: Unbothered by the student union's latest protest turning unruly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting out of hand' scrambles I, NUS and ACTION; NUS is Britain's National Union of Students. 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being nonchalant or carefree means showing no worry or anxiety at all, an exact synonym.

clue.text: Magic spell that principally is used among Indian people

indicators.note: used among means placed amid, inside the other word

parts.note: the Inca nation, the native people of Peru

indicators.note: principally means the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A magic spell principally used among a native tribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' means American Indian: the Inca nation, from Peru. T goes in after INCAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A chant or set of words recited to produce a magical effect.

clue.text: It's clear-cut about wild pig being cause of disease

indicators.note: the trimmed word goes about, round, the pig
cut means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: patent means clear or obvious
a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: Plainly, a wild boar can spread illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clear-cut' looks like one adjective, but 'cut' trims the clear word to PATEN; 'about' wraps it round the pig. 'It's' and 'being' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A germ, virus or other microorganism that produces illness is the agent responsible for it.

clue.text: A South American leader initially welcomed as a hero

indicators.note: a guest welcomed is taken in, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: a Chilean comes from Chile

indicators.note: initially means the first letter

explanation.surface: A South American leader is welcomed initially as a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives L from 'leader', which is 'welcomed' into CHILEAN after CHIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes what is like the Greek warrior of the Trojan War, the model of heroic valour.

clue.text: Firm not out to make money

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
in cricket a batsman not out is still in

explanation.surface: A firm that stays in business keeps making money.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who is 'not out' is still IN at the crease.
explanation.definitionFit: To mint metal currency is literally to manufacture cash, the verb sense here.

clue.text: Flat surface for assembling stone work

parts.note: a tablet is a slab of stone with writing on it
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A level stone slab where you assemble a piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for assembling' joins the definition to the pieces, which are put together in order.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a table is a level surface on which things stand.

clue.text: Drink served hot in saloon maybe

indicators.note: the hot letter goes in the saloon, within the vehicle word

parts.note: a saloon is a type of car, hence the maybe
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A drink is served piping hot in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saloon' looks like a bar, but here it is a saloon car (a sedan). 'served' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Char is British slang for tea, from the Chinese cha, so it is a drink.

clue.text: Examining first of strategies used by prime minister briefly

indicators.note: first of a word means its opening letter

parts.note: George Canning was British prime minister for only a few months in 1827, dying in office

explanation.surface: Examining the first of the strategies the prime minister used, in brief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' seems to say shorten something, but it describes Canning's short time in office. 'used by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking closely at something, or searching through it carefully, is a sense of this verb form.

clue.text: Party sounded extremists out

indicators.note: the extreme letters are put out, so the first and last go

parts.note: fathomed means measured the depth of water, sounded

explanation.surface: A party sounded out the extremists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounded' is not about voice but measuring depth, as with a plumb line.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal reception held in one's own home, a dated name for such a party.

clue.text: Typical! Loo's broken — don't flush

indicators.note: broken means the letters are smashed up and reassembled

parts.note: loo is British slang for a toilet; the 's is no letter

explanation.surface: A toilet out of order, and the advice is not to pull the chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flush' looks like pulling the chain, but it means blushing: stay calm and don't get flustered.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying calm and not showing embarrassment means not going red in the face, a cheeky definition by idiom.

clue.text: Clever enough for investigative work? Not half

indicators.note: not half means one half of the word is dropped, here its first four letters

parts.note: research is careful investigation

explanation.surface: Is someone clever enough to do detective work? Not half!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' looks like the British exclamation meaning very much, but it drops RESE from RESEARCH. 'enough for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch means cunning or knowingly sly, as in an arch smile, close to clever.

clue.text: The end is nigh

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for an ending and an adjective meaning near.

clue.text: I don't believe you cope

definitions.meaning: to manage or get by, as in how are you managing

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both an old expression of disbelief and a way of saying someone manages or gets by.

clue.text: A success in the past

parts.note: a go is a success, as in make a go of it

explanation.surface: A success that's in the past.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means earlier, gone by, back in time.

clue.text: Final examination? These results in particular overwhelm schools' heads

indicators.note: the heads of the words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: Final exam results swamp the head teachers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tripos is the final honours examination at Cambridge University; the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cambridge honours degree examination is a final exam, hence the question mark for an example.

clue.text: 20 to 1 I'll get into Oxford?

parts.note: the answer to 20 down, meaning being home, means in
one alone is sole, single

explanation.surface: A bookmaker's odds of twenty to one on getting into Oxford University.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' is not the university but an oxford, a lace-up shoe, which an inner sole goes into. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A removable inner layer fits inside a shoe, and an oxford is a style of laced leather shoe.

clue.text: Possibly faded flowers I plucked in wide-ranging areas

parts.note: ex means former, past its prime

indicators.note: a letter plucked out is removed

parts.note: pansies are garden flowers

explanation.surface: Faded flowers, plucked by me, across broad stretches of land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plucked' removes I from PANSIES. 'Possibly' is a link warning that EX for 'faded' is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad stretches of open land or sea are wide areas, the plural noun here.
